A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Design2GarmentCode, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures. v1 ends after its references; v3 includes supplementary material. Shared content and material relocated into the supplement can be reliably matched.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original garment-generation simulations and a study involving 30 professional pattern-makers, with quantitative results in Table 1 and qualitative demonstrations.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and reports additional quantitative metrics and supplementary generation and editing results.

M1.justification: The MMUA/DSL-GA pipeline, LoRA program learning, 122-parameter projector, and validation stages remain unchanged in Section 3. The supplementary validation, pose-estimation, and prompting descriptions provide implementation detail without establishing an algorithm or architecture revision.

E1.justification: Both versions use GarmentCodeData and evaluate text-, image-, and sketch-guided generation and garment editing. v3's garment-category counts and additional examples document retained coverage; they do not establish a new dataset, modality, or distinct task.

E2.justification: DressCode remains the text-generation comparator and Sewformer the image-generation comparator in Table 1 and Figures 4–5. TokenHMR is an implementation dependency, while the drafting examples do not introduce a new comparison against the proposed system.

E3.justification: Table 1 adds CLIPScore, F-Score, and Chamfer Distance as evaluation metrics. The original 150 text prompts, 150 images, 30-person study, and stated training settings are retained. Detailed protocols for the new metrics are not supplied.

E4.justification: Figure 19 extends the instruction-editing case studies with additional sequences testing targeted garment modifications. Section 9.1 and Figure 13 also provide a concrete drafting-knowledge example for the capability discussed in v1. No controlled component ablations or systematic robustness studies are added.

E5.justification: Table 1 changes diversity dispersion reporting from variance to standard deviation. All twelve revised subscripts equal the rounded square roots of the earlier variances, such as 2.76 becoming 1.66. Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, seeds, or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: v3 adds objective text-alignment and geometric-accuracy results: Table 1 reports CLIPScores of 0.2386 for DressCode and 0.2438 for Ours, and image-guided F-Scores of 0.708 for Sewformer and 0.829 for Ours, alongside Chamfer distances. Figures 16–19 substantially expand generation and editing outcomes. Original SSR, preference scores, and diversity means remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5 and the DressCode token-length derivation are preserved, with the latter relocated into supplementary Section 8.2. No substantive mathematical definitions, assumptions, proofs, or derivations are added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about multimodal program synthesis, geometric precision, training efficiency, and editable garment design. The added material supports those claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: Section 7 adds specific explanations of incomplete MMUA answers and out-of-range hallucinations, and identifies image-guided generation as particularly benefiting from design comparison. Existing limitations concerning thin straps, unconventional bodices, and stitching are retained in Section 10 and Figure 14.

D1.justification: Sections 7–9 substantially expand documentation: 583 natural-language/code training pairs, a two-loop validation limit, TokenHMR camera/pose estimation, a comparison prompt, parameter-conversion examples, and inference and user-study interfaces. Existing training settings are largely relocated. The explicit code/data-release promise disappears from the abstract, while complete prompts remain promised with the code.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 adds a bounded extension to human-motion and visual-reasoning research, citing works including ChatPose, Symbol-LLM, and HumanVLA; TokenHMR is also newly cited. The central positioning around neurosymbolic generation and GarmentCode remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the main section order are retained. Implementation details and detailed limitations move into supplementary Sections 8 and 10, accompanied by new explanatory subsections and localized related-work, abstract, affiliation, and acknowledgment edits.

P2.justification: v3 adds prompt, interface, drafting-output, and configuration figures, plus four extensive generation/editing galleries. Table 1 gains metric rows, existing main figures are rearranged, and v1's limitation Figure 10 is relocated and enlarged as Figure 14. The visual documentation expands substantially.

improvement.justification: The supplement improves transparency through concrete validation, prompting, implementation, and user-study documentation, while additional results broaden the inspectable evidence. However, the new geometric metrics lack detailed evaluation protocols, limiting their evidential weight. The clearest overall gain is better documentation and illustration of the retained method.
